newsitem.title: USA: US union calls for reform of FAA committee.
newsitem.headline: US union calls for reform of FAA committee.

text.p: An airline union official on Tuesday called for a reform of an outside committee that advises the Federal Aviation Administration, charging the panel was more interested in airlines than in safety.

Patricia Friend, president of the Association of Flight Attendants, said the Aviation Rulemaking Advisory Committee (ARAC) was heavily weighted in favor of the industry and lacked effective representation from public interest groups.
She said the panel was formed with a widely representative membership to advise the FAA on issues from crew fatigue to emergency evacuation, and it was to meet in public session.

Friend told the International Aviation Club that the panel was operating within the law, but much of its work was being done by subcommittees outside the formal committee, which were biased in favor of industry and which held private meetings.

She said industry spends an estimated $2 million a year to staff the subcommittees, where recommendations were fashioned in closed meetings before going to the FAA without an open meeting of the full ARAC.

Friend said, "We know of no instance when a full meeting of the ARAC membership has reviewed and debated the technical details of an ARAC recommendation. Indeed, we know of no full meeting of the ARAC since 1991."
"The practical results of this structure has been a shift from a collaborative approach where all sides have an equal voice to a simple matter of who has the most votes," she said.
The panels often back an easing of regulations, she said.
Friend said the industry expected to recoup money spent on the panels by actions that eliminate or reduce the costs of regulations it deems unnecessary.
"ARAC's bias toward industry threatens to make the FAA's true mission one of promoting safety only when safety interests coincide with the promotion of air commerce," she said.
The ARAC should be kept as an FAA advisory panel but restructured "to make it an appropriate source of advice and information for the FAA," she added.

Friend said the changes should include limiting the ARAC to advising the FAA rather than submitting proposed regulations. Each group should be chaired by an FAA official, there should be wider public membership, and it should meet in public.
She noted that a new law directs the FAA to promote safety only, rather than both aviation and safety.
Friend added that, "Unless such changes are made now, it will be a long time before we see the FAA's recently enacted mandate for a single mission of safety being put into practice."
There was no immediate comment from the FAA.
